title: BYTE-GOLD: mine, label, plant

story: Last month Byte, our review agent, reviewed 411 pull requests in fcp, the product repo, and left 942 comments. A review costs about two dollars and takes about five minutes. Then someone suggests running Byte at medium effort instead of high, which would make every review cheaper. The person who maintains Byte asks the only question that matters: will it miss bugs?

Nobody can answer. We can count Byte's comments, but we cannot say how many real bugs it catches, or how many of its comments were noise. To say whether medium is good enough, we first need to know how good high is, and for that we need a set of pull requests where we already know the right answer.
hook.question: How do we build an honest answer key for a code reviewer, using bugs that really happened in our own repo?

p: Byte is the review agent that already reads every pull request in fcp. When you open a PR or push to it, a GitHub Actions workflow runs on our own runners, and Claude (Opus 5.5 at high effort) reads the diff and the code around it. It answers with findings. A finding is one comment tied to a file and a line, with a severity: high means you would block the merge for it, medium means it is real but not blocking, and low means it is minor. Byte's own code posts the findings as a review; the model never writes to GitHub itself.

Each run uses two containers, the same pattern you met in the lesson about brokers. The broker container holds the GitHub token and answers only read questions about this one PR. The worker container runs Claude with read-only tools that ask the broker, so the model never holds a token. Keep this picture in mind: later lessons in this part change what the worker is allowed to see, which model it runs, and what it posts.

Byte has been running for months, and it keeps careful numbers about itself: reviews, findings, cost and minutes. What it has never had is a test of its quality. Its only eval is a set of 25 small fixtures for one cheap check, the sniff, which a later lesson explains. Nothing measures whether its reviews catch the bugs that matter.

deeper.h: Go deeper: one Byte run, step by step
p: Byte lives in its own repo, RhinoHealth/byte, written in TypeScript like our platform. fcp calls Byte's reusable workflow, review.yml, which runs four jobs in order. The gate decides whether this event deserves a review at all (a draft, a bot or a missing permission means no) and which team's playbook applies. The sniff runs on later pushes and asks whether Byte's open findings were fixed. The review job starts the broker and the worker. The finalize job writes the check run you see on the PR.

The playbooks are plain Markdown files baked into Byte's image, one per team, such as skills/fe/SKILL.md, with a MEMORY.md of lessons from past reviews. Byte also has a fix mode: comment @byte-fix on a PR and it writes a small fix PR into the author's branch. Every run adds a row of numbers (no code, no text) to a telemetry branch, and a weekly job collects the thumbs-up and thumbs-down people give its comments.

read.h: Where the bugs are hiding: our own history
p: Every shipped bug in fcp left two traces. First, a Jira Bug ticket was closed. Second, a fix landed on main as one squashed commit, with a subject like [BE] RH-8123: Dataset check uses the dataset's workgroup (#1932). The lines that fix changed are the lines where the bug lived, so if we ask who wrote those lines before the fix, we find the pull request that introduced the bug. That is the PR Byte should have caught.

git blame answers exactly that question: for every line of a file, it names the commit that last wrote it. The trick is to blame the fix's parent, written fixSha^ in git, which is the code as it was just before the fix. Blame the fix commit itself and every changed line points at the fix. This method has a name, SZZ, after the three researchers who published it. Because fcp squash-merges, each blamed commit's subject ends with (#1874), so the PR number comes straight out of the subject.

The miner is a small script that does this for every fix in the last eighteen months. It reads only the old side of each change (a fix that only adds lines has nothing to blame), and it skips tests, lockfiles and generated code, because a fix there is not a bug in product code.

notes.text: A hunk header looks like @@ -212,7 +212,8 @@. The -212,7 part is the old side: the start line and how many old lines changed.
The diff from the parent to the fix, with zero context lines (-U0), so every hunk holds only changed lines.
Skip hunks that removed nothing (pure additions), and files in SKIP.
Blame only the changed range, at the fix's parent. -w ignores whitespace, -M and -C follow moved and copied lines, so a reformat does not take the blame.
The subject of the blamed commit ends with (#1874): that number is the introducing PR.
Count blamed lines per PR. A PR that wrote ten of the changed lines is a stronger candidate than one that wrote one.

read.h: A person confirms, and writes the answer
p: SZZ is a good guess, not the truth. A fix sometimes tidies a line next to the bug, or the bug was caused by a config change that no diff line shows. So the script only produces candidates, about 300 of them, and people from the frontend and backend guilds check each one in about ten minutes. They open the fix PR, the Bug ticket and the introducing PR, and they keep the candidate only if the cause is visible in the introducing PR's diff. Otherwise they reject it with one word: refactor, config or unclear.

For each kept candidate the labeler writes the golden comment: the file and lines where the bug is, its severity on Byte's own scale, and one or two sentences that describe the defect the way a good reviewer would have said it. Together, the case file is the answer key for one PR.

code.text:
{
  "id": "real-0042",
  "kind": "real",
  "repository": "RhinoHealth/fcp",
  "prNumber": 1874,
  "team": "be",
  "bugKey": "RH-8123",
  "fixPr": 1932,
  "blankBody": false,
  "split": null,
  "golden": [
    {
      "path": "cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/permissions.py",
      "startLine": 212,
      "endLine": 218,
      "severity": "high",
      "defect": "The new object check compares the user's active workgroup instead of the dataset's own workgroup, so a member of another workgroup can read the dataset.",
      "labeler": "<labeler's GitHub login>"
    }
  ]
}

notes.text: real: a bug from history. The other kinds are clean and planted (next section).
The introducing PR. This is the PR Byte reviews when we test it, not the fix PR.
The Jira key only, never the ticket text, because Bug tickets can name customers.
true when the PR's title or body was edited later and now mentions the bug; the body is then left out of the test.
Would you block the merge for it? Then it is high.
The defect in code terms only. A model will read this sentence later, when it decides whether Byte's finding matches.

p: Real bugs measure recall: of the bugs we know, how many did Byte catch? But recall alone can be fooled. A reviewer that comments on every single line catches every bug and is useless, because people stop reading it. So the set also holds clean PRs: PRs merged three months to a year ago, under 600 changed lines, that no later fix ever blamed and nobody reverted. Any high or medium finding on a clean PR is a false alarm, and the bar is at most 0.2 of them per clean PR, so roughly one false alarm in five clean PRs.

History also has gaps. Some bug classes we care about, such as a missing workgroup check or a migration that locks a big table, happened too rarely to measure. For those, a labeler takes a different clean PR and writes a small patch that adds exactly one bug, a planted bug, with its own golden comment. The patch must apply cleanly on that PR's head and look like the code around it: no hinting comments, no TODOs, only fake data.
The target is 240 cases: 120 confirmed real bugs, 60 clean PRs and 60 planted bugs. Together they are called BYTE-GOLD, and they are the fixed exam every future change to Byte must pass.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the answer key stays secret
p: If Byte ever reads a golden comment, every score is worthless, in the same way a student who saw the answer sheet proves nothing by passing. So the cases live in their own private repo, RhinoHealth/byte-gold, which only a few people can read. Byte's GitHub App is never installed on it, because Byte reviews every repo it is installed on.

The miner runs on a person's laptop with a full fcp clone and a read-only Jira token, never in CI. It writes ids, numbers and the Jira key, and nothing from the ticket text. The next lesson makes sure that, when Byte reviews an old PR for the test, it cannot see the fix or anything else that happened later.

lab.title: Mine one bug from a history you write
lab.goal: Build a tiny repo with fcp-style squash commits, find the PR that introduced a bug with blame at the fix's parent, and write its golden comment.

guess.q: A fix commit changed line 6 of src/paging.ts. You run git blame on line 6 at the fix commit itself, not at its parent. Which PR does blame name?

options.text: The PR that introduced the bug
options.why: That PR wrote the old line 6. The fix replaced it, so at the fix commit line 6 belongs to someone else.
At the fix commit, the fix wrote line 6. You must blame the parent (fixSha^) to see who wrote the buggy version.

options.text: The first commit of the repo
options.why: Blame names the last commit that wrote each line, not the first one in history.

follow.say: Create a small history that looks like fcp's: squash commits whose subjects end with the PR number. PR #12 brings a paging bug, PR #15 fixes it.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/scratch && cd ~/academy-labs/scratch && rm -rf gold-lab && mkdir gold-lab && cd gold-lab
git init -q -b main && git config user.name "Lab" && git config user.email lab@example.com && mkdir -p src tests
printf 'export const PAGE_SIZE = 25;\n\nexport const firstPage = <T>(rows: T[]): T[] => rows.slice(0, PAGE_SIZE);\n' > src/paging.ts
git add -A && git commit -q -m "[FE] RH-1190: Projects table shows the first page (#11)"
printf '\nexport const pageOf = <T>(rows: T[], page: number): T[] =>\n  rows.slice(page * PAGE_SIZE, page * PAGE_SIZE + PAGE_SIZE + 1);\n\nexport const pageCount = (total: number): number => Math.ceil(total / PAGE_SIZE);\n' >> src/paging.ts
git commit -q -am "[FE] RH-1207: Projects table pages through every project (#12)"
printf '\nexport const isEmpty = <T>(rows: T[]): boolean => rows.length === 0;\n' >> src/paging.ts
git commit -q -am "[FE] RH-1215: Projects table knows when it is empty (#13)"
sed -i '' 's/PAGE_SIZE + PAGE_SIZE + 1)/PAGE_SIZE + PAGE_SIZE)/' src/paging.ts
printf 'import { pageOf } from "../src/paging.ts";\n' > tests/paging.test.ts
git add -A && git commit -q -m "[FE] RH-1301: Every page shows 25 projects, not 26 (#15)"
git log --oneline
follow.see:
0b2ee27 [FE] RH-1301: Every page shows 25 projects, not 26 (#15)
8aeb727 [FE] RH-1215: Projects table knows when it is empty (#13)
a91c211 [FE] RH-1207: Projects table pages through every project (#12)
f1abfda [FE] RH-1190: Projects table shows the first page (#11)
(your hashes are different)

follow.say: Look at the fix with zero context lines, because the hunk header tells you which old lines changed.
Blame old line 6 at the fix's parent, then read that commit's subject. This is SZZ by hand.
follow.do:
git blame -L 6,6 HEAD^ -- src/paging.ts
git log -1 --format=%s $(git blame -L 6,6 --porcelain HEAD^ -- src/paging.ts | head -1 | cut -c1-40)
follow.see:
a91c211d (Lab 2026-10-16 05:18:42 +0300 6)   rows.slice(page * PAGE_SIZE, page * PAGE_SIZE + PAGE_SIZE + 1);
[FE] RH-1207: Projects table pages through every project (#12)

follow.say: Now let a script do it for every hunk. Save this as mine.ts (it is the miner from the Understand step, for the current folder) and run it on the fix.
Write the answer key for this case, the golden comment, and read it back with jq.
follow.do:
mkdir -p cases/real-0001 && cat > cases/real-0001/case.json <<'EOF'
{
  "id": "real-0001",
  "kind": "real",
  "prNumber": 12,
  "bugKey": "RH-1301",
  "fixPr": 15,
  "golden": [
    {
      "path": "src/paging.ts",
      "startLine": 5,
      "endLine": 6,
      "severity": "medium",
      "defect": "pageOf slices one row too many, so every page shows 26 projects and repeats the first row of the next page."
    }
  ]
}
EOF
jq -r '"\(.id) \(.kind) PR #\(.prNumber): \(.golden | length) golden comment(s), \(.golden[0].severity)"' cases/real-0001/case.json
follow.see: real-0001 real PR #12: 1 golden comment(s), medium

lab.build: Plant a bug. PR #11 is clean: no fix ever blamed it. Check out its head with git switch --detach ":/RH-1190", change rows.slice(0, PAGE_SIZE) to rows.slice(1, PAGE_SIZE) in src/paging.ts, and save the change with git diff > cases/planted-0001/planted.patch. Restore the file (git checkout -- src), and prove the patch applies on that head with git apply --check. Then write cases/planted-0001/case.json with kind planted, prNumber 11 and a golden comment on line 3. Finally, run git switch main and try git apply --check again: why does it fail there?
checks: git blame at HEAD^ names the commit whose subject ends with (#12).
jq reads your real-0001 case and prints medium.
git apply --check cases/planted-0001/planted.patch prints nothing and exits 0 on PR #11's head.
On main the same check fails, because the patch only fits the PR it was written for.

solution.text:
git switch -q --detach ":/RH-1190"
sed -i '' 's/rows.slice(0, PAGE_SIZE)/rows.slice(1, PAGE_SIZE)/' src/paging.ts
mkdir -p cases/planted-0001 && git diff > cases/planted-0001/planted.patch
git checkout -q -- src
git apply --check cases/planted-0001/planted.patch && echo applies
cat > cases/planted-0001/case.json <<'EOF'
{
  "id": "planted-0001",
  "kind": "planted",
  "prNumber": 11,
  "plantedPatch": "planted.patch",
  "plantedClass": "off-by-one",
  "golden": [
    { "path": "src/paging.ts", "startLine": 3, "endLine": 3, "severity": "high",
      "defect": "firstPage starts at index 1, so the first project is never shown." }
  ]
}
EOF
git switch -q main
git apply --check cases/planted-0001/planted.patch   # error: patch does not apply (main has more lines after line 3)

lab.fix: A teammate made the miner "simpler" by blaming the fix commit instead of its parent. Run sed 's/`${fixSha}^`, "--", path/fixSha, "--", path/' mine.ts > fix-mine.ts && node fix-mine.ts HEAD: it prints Map(1) { 15 => 1 } and names the fix PR as the culprit. Find the one argument that changed and explain why it gives this answer.
explain: Why does the miner blame fixSha^ and not fixSha?
Why do the miner's results stay candidates until a person confirms them?
What would happen to the score if BYTE-GOLD had real bugs but no clean PRs?
lab.done: mine.ts finds PR #12 for the fix, your two case files exist, and you can explain why the planted patch only applies on its own PR.

check.q: A fix commit on main changed three lines. Which commit does the miner blame to find the PR that introduced the bug?

options.text: The fix commit, on the lines it added
options.why: Those lines were written by the fix, so blame would name the fix PR every time.
Later changes to the same lines would take the blame, and the trail to the bug would be lost.

options.text: The fix's parent, on the old lines the fix changed
options.why: The parent is the code just before the fix, so blame names who wrote the buggy lines.

check.q: Why does BYTE-GOLD include 60 clean PRs that have no bug at all?

options.text: To count false alarms: a reviewer that flags everything would catch every bug and still be useless
options.why: Recall alone rewards noise. Findings on clean PRs show how often Byte cries wolf.

options.text: To make the set bigger, so the numbers are more stable
options.why: Size helps, but clean PRs have a specific job: measuring noise, which real bugs cannot measure.

options.text: To give Byte easy cases that raise its score
options.why: Clean PRs can only lower the score, through false alarms. They are not a reward.

check.q: A Bug was fixed by a commit that only added a missing null check and changed no existing line. What does the miner find?

options.text: The PR that wrote the function around the new check
options.why: The miner only blames old lines the fix changed. Context lines are not in a -U0 diff.

options.text: Nothing: a pure addition has no old lines to blame, so this bug needs a person, or a planted case of the same class
options.why: SZZ cannot see a bug that is a missing line. That is one reason planted bugs exist.
The miner blames the parent, and it skips hunks that removed nothing, so the fix PR never appears.

p: BYTE-GOLD lives in a private repo, RhinoHealth/byte-gold, readable by Sean, Nave (who maintains Byte) and the labelers; the Byte App is never installed there. The miner, scripts/gold-mine.ts, sits in RhinoHealth/byte next to scripts/sniff-fixtures.ts and runs from an operator's laptop with a full fcp clone, gh and a read-only Jira token.

It starts from the JQL project = RH AND issuetype = Bug AND statusCategory = Done AND resolved >= -540d, matches the keys in squash subjects, adds every Revert commit and subjects with fix or hotfix, scores candidates by blamed lines, days to fix and PR size, drops PRs over 2,000 changed lines, and writes candidates/real.jsonl and candidates/clean.jsonl (about 300 and 150). The guilds then label in batches, one byte-gold PR per batch for Sean to review: frontend/ and ohif/ go to the FE guild, cloud/, client/, sdk/ and common/ to the BE guild.

tickets.why: The miner: SZZ blame at the fix's parent, the candidate lists and the clean pool.
Labelling 120 real bugs and writing their golden comments in case.json.
Confirming 60 clean PRs and planting 60 bugs with planted.patch.

words.plain: One review comment from Byte, tied to a file and a line, with a severity: high, medium or low.
Find the change that introduced a bug by blaming the lines its fix changed, at the fix's parent.
The answer for one case: where the bug is, how bad it is, and what a reviewer should have said.
A high or medium finding on a clean PR, where there was nothing wrong.
One realistic bug a person adds to a clean PR with a small patch, for bug classes history has too few of.
The fixed set of 240 cases (real, clean and planted) that Byte is scored on.

review.q: From memory: the three kinds of case in BYTE-GOLD and what each one measures.
review.a: Real bugs from history and planted bugs measure recall (did Byte catch the known bug?). Clean PRs measure false alarms (high or medium findings where nothing was wrong).

review.q: A labeler opens a candidate and cannot see the bug in the introducing PR's diff. What should they do, and why not keep it anyway?
review.a: Reject it with one word (refactor, config, unclear). A wrong answer key makes every recall number wrong; a smaller, correct set is better.

review.q: Why does case.json hold the Jira key but never the ticket text?
review.a: Bug tickets can name customers, and a model reads the case files when it scores Byte. Ids and a code-only defect sentence are all the scoring needs.

remember: To measure a reviewer, use bugs you already know: blame each fix's parent to find the PR that brought the bug, let a person confirm it, and add clean PRs so noise counts too.
